utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution is cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. If Your Honours please, before I continue with my cross-examination, there is an evidential issue that has arisen and that the Prosecution wishes to address you on before it continues with its cross-examination and Mr. Re will make that application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution has an application. The application is simply this: I'll just tell Your Honours what the application is and then address you on it. The application is to seek the Trial Chamber's leave to cross-examine the accused Mr. Tadic on matters which were in the records of interview, the telephone interviews, which the Trial Chamber ruled upon in the order of 11th of September, 2001. For the purposes of the -- it only goes to my submission will be only directed to credibility and prior inconsistent statement, not being used as part of the Prosecution case. For the purposes of this application, I will hand to Your Honours a copy of the decision for Your Honours' ease of following it and for the purposes of the application the telephone interviews I'll hand you a copy of those so that you can follow the points I wish to address you on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: First of all I hand up three copies of the Trial Chamber's decision of the 11th of September, 2001, entitled decision on Prosecutor's request to add further exhibits to the confidential Prosecution exhibit list filed on the 9th of April, 2001 and I have some copies for my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic? You have something to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally, I cannot object the Prosecution giving their arguments at the very beginning but what I'm objecting to is that they quote any part of that interview in order to support their argumentation before the Trial Chamber rules on it. So I would request that the argumentation of the OTP be restricted strictly to legal matters, not to factual matters and then I will present my argumentation once I hear what they have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think it's better to allow the Prosecution to put before the Chamber what they want to put before the Chamber and then the Trial Chamber will be able to decide on the next step to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: For the purposes of the application only and I assure my learned friend Mr. Lukic of that, I hand up copies of the telephone interview with Mr. Tadic and the OTP on the 26th of April, 1996, telephone interview with Mr. Tadic, a transcript of it, the 29th of April, 1996, and thirdly, the telephone interview with Mr. Tadic on the 22nd of May, 1996. Copies for the Trial Chamber and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I can take Your Honours to page 3 of the decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. Your Honours, I am stating my objection again. I don't think that this document should be analysed in this way. The Prosecution wants to present something to the Trial Chamber without explaining why they want to do that. I've explained very clearly when I objected the first time what were the reasons. If you remember, the reason was that the OTP did not apply the rules of procedure properly, because they did not inform the accused of the charges, and that was the basis for the Trial Chamber's ruling. They objected to this kind of attitude of the OTP with respect to the accused. Forcing him to take the interview without informing him of the charges, and now they are trying to bring in the interview again. Let them state what their reasons are without quoting the interview. Trial Chamber's ruling was based on the fact that you did not wish to be informed of the interview, which was taken illegally from the accused, and now, the Prosecution is trying to present that very interview to the Trial Chamber. When the Prosecution informed us how they interviewed Tadic before informing him of the charges and one of the most fundamental rules of the Statute is Rule 21 where it says that the accused needs to be informed of the charges. Now they are trying to go around this. They want to you read the interview, which you have already declared to be illegally obtained. Let them present their arguments first. If they have something that goes against the credibility of that witness, they can put questions to the witness without presenting the conclusions to us first. I insist on hearing the arguments of the OTP for raising this matter now. They cannot raise the matter by simply giving the Trial Chamber the document to read which the Trial Chamber declined to be informed of.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was not reading from the interviews, I was referring Your Honours to page 3 of the decision and the decision does not say that it was illegally obtained. What my friend said was just wrong. I was taking Your Honours to the basis for the exclusion and I was going to address you on that. And then come to the evidentiary issues which you as professional Judges must look into before deciding on the admissibility of the motion which I haven't yet got to because of my learned friend's objection to me even addressing you on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more matter, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can you just wait a minute? Can you just sit down? Mr. Re, the Trial Chamber wants to know whether these interviews are the same interviews, the basis of this decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the bases of the application but the application is only put on the basis of impeachment in relation to credibility and a prior inconsistent statement, not consciousness of guilt. It was excluded for one reason. I have case law which I will take you to if I can get to that. The application is to allow the Prosecution to cross-examine Mr. Tadic as to inconsistencies between various statements he has made on various issues which goes only to his credibility and believability as a witness, and when the Trial Chamber has to decide his credibility versus the versions of other witnesses who may not have made statements which the Trial Chamber could decide to be inconsistent as to who you will believe on various issues. None of these issues are in the nature of a confession or in the nature of an admission which is, "I committed the crime or I did not commit the crime." These only go to a number of inconsistencies the Prosecution would say between various versions the defendant has given of different issues in the case but none of them being the big one, none of them being the complete admission to the offence. That is that is the nature of the application. It is limited only to credibility. Prior inconsistent statement, impeachment. It does not go to consciousness of guilt. And Mr. Lukic said that the Trial Chamber excluded it on the basis of it being illegally obtained. This is just -- that is very far from the truth. If you look at the decision, page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re? You finished your legal argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm trying to start it. Mr. Lukic, I think, wants to object again before I finish my argument. He's on his feet so I'll sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought you have said so because you are dealing -- you are stating that you only want to use them as to credibility and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Completely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The basis upon -- this is what I was taking Your Honours to the basis upon as I can see, as the Prosecution understands the Trial Chamber's exclusion was not that it was an involuntary statement which of course would render it inadmissible but only as -- on a discretionary basis as to the way it was obtained. That is a -- not a violation but it was obtained in such a way as the Trial Chamber considered it to be unfair to use it in the Prosecution case against the accused, because the Trial Chamber found that the accused did not fully -- was not satisfied the accused did not fully appreciate the seriousness of the indictment, nor understand fully the nature of the indictment and the proceedings. Now that is obviously a pure -- a discretionary decision. It's not a -- based upon fairness grounds rather than voluntariness. The three interviews which I understand that the Trial Chamber had in front of them for the purposes of deciding the Prosecutor's original application to use it in the Prosecution case, reveal very clearly that firstly Mr. Tadic was the person who initiated the contact with the OTP, telephoning them, in the -- all three of the interviews he had his lawyer present with him, the second one the lawyer came in after the first few minutes, maybe five, ten minutes, into the interview, he was cautioned, and the procedures were entirely consistent with Rule 43 for the interview of a suspect, although of course he wasn't a suspect, he was an indicted accused at the time. And each of the three interviews reveals the cautioning, the reading of the rights, the establishment by the OTP as to whether Mr. Tadic was voluntarily speaking to the OTP, whether he wanted a lawyer, and so on. And it transpired that his lawyer was there with him. In the last record of interview his lawyer even spoke to the OTP over the phone. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that should put aside in my submission any concerns Your Honours may have as to even now the voluntary nature of what he said. What we look at is whether or not, if it's not part of the Prosecution case, and has been excluded, the Prosecutor or another party is entitled to cross-examine the witness or the accused as to any differences between any statements he has made in the past and his -- that's hearsay evidence of course, and his in court testimony. And of course it would operate in a common law jurisdiction as an exception to the hearsay rule, a prior inconsistent statement of an out of court representation of a witness. The Prosecutor's submission here is that it does not infringe any of his rights under the Statute because it is not being used, the right to be informed of the charge which the Prosecutor says he was informed in general terms of the nature of the charge, in the first record of interview in the first couple of pages he even says I've been indicted for -- I've been indicted for what he says the ethnic cleansing in Bosanski Samac. He was fairly clear that he was aware of the circumstances of the indictment and there was an exchange of information between him and the OTP, as Your Honours can see from the record of interview -- sorry, from the telephone interviews where Mr. Tadic either through his lawyer or himself sent a large volume of material to the OTP, mainly consisting, I think, of exchange lists. So there was an ongoing dialogue so to speak, after he was indicted, after he'd been informed he was indicted and was aware he was facing charges of quote ethnic cleansing unquote. Now the Prosecutor says that in those three telephone interviews which he made voluntarily after having been informed of his right not to speak to the Prosecutor, that it was being taped, having obtained his consent in all three to the taping of the interviews, and having his lawyer present, he gave information to the OTP which the Prosecutor says is inconsistent with some of the answers, some of the testimony he's given, over the last few days. We have done some comparative law research to look for -- sorry, I withdraw that. The starting point is ICTY and perhaps ICTR jurisprudence on this particular point. Our searches have been unable to reveal any direct precedent in the ICTY on this particular point or any ruling of a Trial Chamber. Our searches have been unable to reveal but sometimes there are oral rulings which are hard to detect. We have done a survey of the major common law systems. As far as we can see it's not really a matter which is applicable in civil law systems because of the role of the investigating judge or the larger role of judges in civil law, criminal trials, and their role being determinative of the -- from an earlier stage, and the use that can be made of it, of an inconsistency. And it would appear that in the major civil systems it wouldn't really make a difference, the judge would be able to use it if he or she wished, having had the material in front of him or her for the duration of the trial, all of the material. The most relevant jurisdiction we can find or the most relevant area on point is in the United States, and the exception to the Miranda rules for violations of the 5th Amendment where an accused has given information to the police after not having been cautioned. Now, that information cannot be used against him or her in court because it's been obtained in violation of the 5th Amendment and Miranda -- and Miranda but the case law holds that this does not prevent the Prosecution or another party impeaching the witness with that material at a later point if what they -- if they say something contrary to the material which was excluded. The relevant cases to which I refer Your Honours, and I'll hand up the cases, the case two United States Supreme Court cases of Harris and New York, the citation is 401, U.S., 222, and the case of Calder -- just excuse me one moment, I have it. The case of - I'm sorry - Walder, W-A-L-D-E-R and the United States, 347, U.S., 62. I hand up these two cases and provide copies to my colleagues on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I could take Your Honours first to the case of Walder and the United States, Your Honours can see from the head note on the first page the circumstances of the case. That is what -- that is it relates to the credibility of an accused and the possession of narcotics. The relevant passage is in the second page of the copy I've handed up, you see on the second half of the page, it's at page 356 of the citation. There is a paragraph heading 2, "It is one thing to say that the government cannot make an affirmative use of evidence unlawfully obtained" -- and I just interpolate here that there is no issue despite what my friend said, that the evidence which Your Honours excluded on a discretionary basis was illegally or unlawfully obtained. It was a discretionary fairness exclusion. I go back to the judgement "It is quite another to say that the defendant can turn the illegal method by which evidence in the government's possession was obtained to his own advantage. And provide himself with a shield against contradiction of his untruths. Such an extension of the Weeks doctrine would be a perversion of the 4th" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll repeat that last sentence, "Such extension of the Weeks, W-E-E-K-S, doctrine would be a perversion of the 4th Amendment." The next paragraph outlines the circumstances and I take you -- Your Honours can read that and I take you to the last sentence on that page: "Beyond that, however, there is hardly justification for letting the defendant" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: "Beyond that, however, there is hardly justification for letting the defendant affirmatively resort to perjurious testimony in reliance on the government's disability to challenge his credibility." And that really is the situation here, that the Prosecution's hands are tied behind their back if it has material excluded only on fairness grounds which may suggest that the defendant is not being truthful in his evidence before the Trial Chamber. The second case is Harris and New York, again a U.S. Supreme Court decision. The basis of the decision was that the -- a statement of the accused was held inadmissible because the defendant had not been ruled -- advised of his rights to counsel and to remain silent prior to making the statement but otherwise, it satisfied legal standards of trustworthiness, the Supreme Court held that it was properly usable for impeachment purposes to attack the credibility of the defendant's trial testimony. The passages I take Your Honours to for the purposes of this application on the second page of the copy I've handed up, which is at 224 of the reported judgement, second paragraph, on the second half of the page, halfway down, "Miranda barred the Prosecution from making its case with statements of an accused made while in custody prior to having or effectively waiving counsel. It does not follow from Miranda that evidence inadmissible against an accused in the Prosecution's case in chief is barred for all purposes, provided, of course, that the trustworthiness of the evidence satisfies legal standards." And then the Court in the next paragraph affirms the quotation I read to you a moment ago from Walder. And over the page, the second paragraph, with the paragraph heading 1, "Every criminal defendant is privileged to testify in his own defence or to refuse to do so but that privilege cannot be construed to include the right to commit perjury." And the top of the second half of the page, the second column, "The shield provided by Miranda can not be perverted into a licence to use perjury by way of a defence free from the risk of confrontation with prior inconsistent utterances. We hold, therefore, that petitioner's credibility was appropriately impeached by use of his earlier conflicting statements." The Prosecution says that the accused has given inconsistent -- sorry, has given testimony which is inconsistent with statements he made in each of the three prior records of interview. Sorry, the telephone interviews, which I've handed up for the purposes only of this application. In broad categories, they are in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object. I am listening to the Prosecution and I will say what I think after they finish but I'm opposed to the Prosecution bringing out their arguments, what the witness said in one way then and in another way now. So I'm asking the Prosecution, please, to finish with their argument so that I can respond and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know that the Prosecution have finished their legal argument, and now they are going to quote whatever the statements are. I didn't realise that. So that's why I was not prepared to allow to you speak. I thought the Prosecution is still continuing with their legal arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll conclude my legal arguments, I was going to take Your Honours to the basis for the Prosecution making the application being what we say are inconsistencies, however I'll just conclude the legal argument which is -- or summarise it, which is the Prosecution does not, and I assure my defence colleagues of this, would not intend to use it as evidence of consciousness of guilt. That is the defendant lied because the defendant was -- had a guilty conscience or guilty mind or had a reason to lie. The Prosecution would only seek to make use of what we say, and it's up to the Trial Chamber of course to judge, are inconsistencies between various versions to impeach his credibility, and this is particularly important in situations where a witness may have given evidence on an issue contrary to the defendant's testimony, the accused's testimony, which may be inconsistent with something in an earlier utterance which has been excluded on a discretionary basis, and when the Trial Chamber has to assess who is more believable on different issues, the Trial Chamber should have before it all statements by any witness or an accused in relation -- as long as they are voluntary, in relation to the issue which the Trial Chamber has to decide, and this is particularly important when deciding the competing credibilities between two witnesses or the accused and a witness, either of his own -- either a Defence witness or a Prosecution witness, especially when there is no corroboration from anywhere else on those points. Sometimes it's the only thing which a court or Trial Chamber can look at in determining who is more believable is whether the Prosecution is entitled to submit at the end a witness or the defendant, accused, is unbelievable on this issue or another because of the following. That is the limited use which the Prosecution would seek to make by cross-examining the accused on parts of his prior -- what we say are inconsistent statements. Those are the legal arguments, we put it clearly there is no illegality, the Prosecution says no violation of the Statute. The decision doesn't reflect a violation of the Statute. It reflects a discretionary exclusion on the basis of fairness which the Prosecution says would bring it in, would open it, to allow the Prosecution to cross-examine or another party on the basis of the U.S. Supreme Court -- the United States practice, after something has been excluded for a technical -- a violation of someone's rights but it is otherwise a voluntary statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Re, concerning the Harris and New York case, I see there are four very renowned Supreme Court of the United States Justices dissenting in that case. Have you appended any of the dissents to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. I can obtain them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm sure we can obtain them too in the library but as I say there are four very strong, all Supreme Court of the United States Justices are, but we do have very -- four who are dissenting so this was not an unanimous decision obviously on this point and a second question that I have is this is a 1970 decision. The Walder case is 1953. Have there been any developments since 1973 concerning this issue, the fruit of the poisonous tree as Americans like to call it? And a third point, quite obviously we are not bound by decisions of United States Supreme Court or any other domestic jurisdiction. We are an International Tribunal so from the point of view of comparative reference, I think we should have case law cited to us from other countries other than just the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can my colleague Mr. Weiner address you on the U.S. Supreme Court point? The Prosecution has endeavoured to obtain comparative research on this particular point. We have not been able to find anything particularly -- exactly on this point. There is some English law but the Pace Act - the Police and Criminal Evidence Act - has basically overturned a common law position contrary to what we are arguing and in my submission, that probably wouldn't be very helpful. We can endeavour to find more. We've looked. We've surveyed jurisdictions Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei, Australia, Kenya, India, even Canada. And the Canadian -- there was a Canadian Supreme Court case which appeared to be contrary but it related to consciousness of guilt as opposed to impeachment on the basis of credibility. We couldn't find anything in Canada and we looked, which was directly on point but my learned friend Mr. Weiner can certainly address you on the American aspect better than I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour, this has been the United States law since the Walder case, since 1954. This has been held repeatedly throughout all federal jurisdictions and throughout the States within the United States. In fact, I argued one of these types of cases in 1983 relating to guns and drugs, where evidence -- where information had been excluded from trial, where the defendant got on the witness stand and lied, and the court then changed the decision or reviewed its decision and said we will allow you to use that information which had been rejected strictly on the terms for impeachment. It was a non-published decision in 1983 before the Massachusetts appeals court which was a successful decision. I could get the name if the Court would like but this has been the decision -- this has been the view of the United States since the Walder case, that there is no shield for perjury. Evidence which has been excluded may be used whether it is a 4th Amendment and these are constitutional violations. The Walder decision concerned a 4th Amendment violation, which the right of search and seizure and the Harris versus New York concerned a violation relating to admissability of statements, 5th Amendment related statements. And in each of those areas the statements were later to be used and that is the position of the United States for approximately 50 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, from everything that we have heard so far from the other side, it only confirms my position that the Prosecution is following the wrong road and is trying, via the back door, to do something on which the Chamber has already ruled. Why? The entire arguments of the Prosecution go in favour of what you have said and what I have said and what I'm going to repeat now. It's not up to the Prosecution or the Defence to interpret your decision. Perhaps we could interpret some other Chamber's decision but you, as the Chamber that reached this decision of 11th of September, 2001, know best whether this was a formal or a substantial decision. According to what I think, what you said in the passage before last, on page 3, and you said, [In English] integrity of the process, [Interpretation] does not mean that it is missed procedural thing that the Prosecution didn't carry out during that interview. I think that you have noted the seriousness of such an interview, and the facts which could appear as evidence in the course of the case itself. What I stated then and I am stating now, not going into the broad practice referred to by the Prosecution, I'm going to cite one and fundamental act which is probably a key act in your proceedings, and that is Rule 21 of the Statute. What I said then, item 4, -- 4(A), "The accused must be informed in detail about the nature and the reasons of the charges against him." That is the key. And without this right, there can be no interview with any person, if they happen to be accused, and if there is an indictment against that person. That is the catch. That is what you said that we would not permit in this -- in these proceedings, any catches. The accused was Miroslav Tadic, there was a public indictment issued against him, the Prosecution conducted an interview with him but did not inform him in detail about the charges against him. And now the Prosecution is using that -- those allegations, wishing to compare them with the allegations from this case. What the Prosecution would like to do, and the Chamber and I agree, of course, is that one of the main tasks of this Tribunal is to confirm the credibility and the consistency of statements. He needs to be informed about the allegations and he needs -- these need to be confirmed with evidence of other witnesses, and proof, and these have to be done with something that is permissible to be compared with. You have said that these things are not permissible and not to be used for comparison. The Prosecution has said that it was a mistake, quote unquote, because he was not informed of all the charges but that all the other rights of the accused he was informed about that he had a counsel and that he was informed of his rights. I'm now asking my learned friends from the Prosecution why would anybody need a counsel if the counsel or the person were not aware of what this person is charged with? What right is being met here? Why would anybody need to be informed of their rights if they are not informed of the allegations against them? And because of such an interview, some possible facts were stated, upon which the Prosecution wishes to deal with credibility issues. I think that here we have a flagrant violation of Rule 21 of the Statute, which the Prosecution accepted because, in the ultimate instance, they did not appeal your decision. The Prosecution, without any objection, accepted your ruling, your decision, Your Honours, and now are trying to introduce -- reintroduce this. The position of Miroslav Tadic's Defence is based exclusively on the Statute and on your decision. Nothing has happened or changed for this decision to be reviewed and changed again. Opening up this interview in order to check the consistency means checking facts, and facts which were provided in one way and cannot be compared with facts that you have determined were not given in the proper procedure. And finally, I would like to say as far as procedure is concerned, if the Prosecution wanted to initiate this earlier, I will wait, of course, for the decision of the Chamber but this would lead us to a dramatic situation regarding the rights of the accused and so on but this is something that I do not wish to dwell on now. I think the matter is crystal clear. In order to check consistency, we can compare that with facts which the Trial Chamber views as suitable for comparison, but because one of the basic fundamental rights was violated, and I do not need to remind the Chamber that this provision of the Statute is based on all fundamental human rights decisions about basic -- all the charters, the basic Declaration on Human Rights and others, in any of these charters, the accused has the right to be informed in detail about the charges against him. How can Miroslav Tadic know what ethnic cleansing is in the view of the Prosecution if he had not seen the indictment? So such an interview, which was -- if I were the Prosecutor, I would bury deep in some drawer, they are trying to use it now at this point. And I really very strongly object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour on the same issue, because it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic -- you are not the counsel for Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour but very briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, I will not allow you to make any submissions on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's a fact also general legal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. Your client gave evidence, this issue didn't arise. It doesn't touch him and these interviews were done with the accused Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are not co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: They relate to the case law and to the fundamental issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. No problem. I concur with your decision, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will adjourn and we will notify the parties when we shall resume the proceedings. --- Break taken at 9.50 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has considered the oral motion by the Prosecution on their application for leave to use the interviews, the subject matter of the decision of the Trial Chamber on 11 September, 2001. We have also considered the submissions of the Defence, and we have decided that the motion should be rejected. The reasons will be given in writing in due course. So the cross-examination continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, yesterday you said that your assessment of the events of the night of the 16th and 17th was that the town was under attack. You recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And do you agree that essentially, on Friday last, you described these events, you heard shooting at about 2.30 from the foot bridge, shooting spread to other parts of the town, and at dawn, the episode where your house came under fire occurred? That's a fair assessment of what you said, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your reaction on the night of -- sorry, on the 17th, was to telephone the 4th Detachment headquarters across the road. You were informed that the commander, Mr. Antic, had gone to Pelagicevo, he called you back in the afternoon, told to you do nothing? That's correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Prosecutor to quote from the transcript. I don't believe that the witness stated it exactly in that way, so I would like that to be quoted, if the Prosecutor is referring to what this witness stated, then he should also tell us where was that recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't have to do that with respect, but I am happy to oblige.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because the question was understood by the defendant, and he answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Perhaps to not use up any more time, Mr. Lukic, I think you'll find the evidence in the LiveNote transcript at page 74 onwards from Friday, the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Essentially, though, essentially, Mr. Tadic, you did nothing that -- in response, other than to make the briefest of inquiries and the 4th Detachment did nothing on the 17th, nothing that you were able to discern?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said yes to your previous question, because doing nothing and waiting for orders are two quite similar things. I personally didn't do anything and as for the 4th Detachment, I don't know what it did, what orders it received. I know that I personally did not receive any orders but the 4th Detachment could have received orders in view of its position and it didn't have to receive orders. It depended on the commander. Some parts could have been issued orders and some parts not -- so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you were in the command of the 4th Detachment, you were the assistant commander for logistics. You received no orders to do anything positive on the day of the 17th, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither positive nor negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Well, thank you. Now, did you report the shooting that you had heard during the night to the command of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, because they were able to hear the shooting also. I will repeat again that at the time the phones weren't working and one couldn't use them to report anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were still --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have just found in the transcript something to which I objected just a minute ago. The witness said that he had spoken to his commander on the 17th at 11.00 a.m. whereas the Prosecutor said that the witness had stated that they talked to each other in the afternoon. This is why I wanted this to be shown to the witness, when we are talking about these dates, the hour is very important, and I think that this should be presented to the witness. This is on page 15213, line 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Before I go there --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, on the 14th of February, Friday the 14th of February, referring to page 76 of the transcript, your counsel asked you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Will Your Honours just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: On the -- last Friday, the 14th of February, your counsel asked you, "The next day, Radovan called me and I went across the street I went there. Question: We are talking about the 18th of April? Answer: Yes, I went to see him since the phones were working. I had already called some people and asked them what was going on and the people told me so I knew what happened. So I went to see Radovan he said the commander of the tactical group ordered that a part of the 4th Detachment takes the border areas around the Bosna River and a part of the 4th Detachment should go about collecting the illegal weapons." So you spoke to -- you spoke to the commander, Mr. Radovan Antic, on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And page 75, your counsel asked you questions about the events of the 17th, he asked you if you left your house, you said, I didn't go anywhere, the command was across the road, you could just yell out to them, you called them on the phone, you were told that the commander had gone to Pelagicevo, he had not said anything regarding about any activity, told that you had better stay at home, later Radovan came back, told me there was no need for me to come and that he would call you when he needed you. That's a fair assessment of what happened on the 17th. In fact it's your own words, page 75 of the transcript? Now, that's a fair assessment of what happened, isn't it, on the 17th? According to you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, let's get back to your informing the command or not informing the command of what you had seen and observed on the night of the 16th and 17th. You didn't tell the command of the 4th Detachment of the shooting, now you say that was because they had seen it themselves or heard it themselves. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because both them and I have ears and we can hear what's going on. Other people have stated here as well that they had heard shooting that night so why wouldn't they hear it? The house of Radovan Antic is much closer to the bridge than mine, so he could have heard it just as I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What about the shots being fired at your house? Did you report to the command of the 4th Detachment that your house had been fired upon, that you had almost been killed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did inform him, I don't remember the details, but I probably did it when I saw him and I told him that among other things, this had happened as well. I wouldn't have omitted mentioning that but he had no comments to offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you report to Mr. Zaric, the assistant commander for security in the 4th Detachment, of the shooting that you'd heard and of the attack that your house had come under?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might have told him about it but I don't remember. It wasn't necessary to inform him because he had probably heard it from other people. He knew what was going on. I didn't inform him officially, Mr. Zaric, this and this had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, the town is under attack. That's your assessment. The town is under attack, gun fire has been heard. Your house has been shot at. Bullets have been fired in your direction. You are in the command of the 4th Detachment. You seem to have adopted a fairly casual approach to dealing with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't attribute much significance to this because I could see that shooting at my house was just an incident that was over quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So you weren't too concerned about hearing gun fire in the town in the middle of the night? You weren't too concerned about your house coming -- having come under fire? You weren't too concerned about having narrowly escaped death?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I was concerned but not as concerned as you depict it. I wasn't gripped by panic --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding these incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is that because you knew precisely what was going on on the night of the 16th and 17th of April, you knew exactly what was happening, you knew that there was a takeover in progress, and that you were participating in that? Is that the reason for your lack of deep concern?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that. I simply was not concerned. Now, the fact that you're presenting it in your way is something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And again, from what you could see and observe, the 4th command or rather the command of the 4th command was not too concerned either, because Mr. Radovan Antic left no orders that you were aware of on the 17th for you to follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, calling for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's a matter of pure -- pure fact. He's being asked the 4th command left -- let me rephrase it and put the question in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment left -- gave you no specific orders, did it, on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no orders whatsoever. I had no orders. It could be concluded that the commander didn't have them either because you know that very early that morning, he went to Pelagicevo to see the commander, so had he had orders on the 17th in the morning he wouldn't have gone to Pelagicevo which is some 40 kilometres away to receive possible instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment had means of communications in its possession, didn't it? Radios, telephones?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, telephones, it did have telephones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What about radios, radio communications, walkie-talkies, radio sets, the sort of things armies and soldiers have as a matter of course? It had those facilities as well, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't have those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are you telling the Chamber -- are you telling the Judges that the 4th Detachment didn't have radio sets, didn't have any communication means, this army that existed in 1992, did not have any means of wireless communication?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, that wasn't the army. These people were reservists with very, very limited duties. Therefore, they didn't have those facilities that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: They had uniforms, did they not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some did but they didn't wear the uniforms. Those uniforms were kept in suitcases or in wardrobes at home. Those were reserve uniforms, reserve garments that they had to put on at a certain time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. What about the weapons? Did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did have weapons, but those weapons were treated similarly as uniforms. They were not worn around town, they were kept where they believed it was safest to keep it, away from family members and children and so on. They had to secure the weapon in order to prevent the children from getting a hold of it because these people had their jobs and they had to go away and work during daytime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. So incidentally, were the weapons also kept in suitcases or stored somewhere safe?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were very safe. For the reasons that I have just given you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How many men were in the 4th Detachment, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, there were fewer men and later on, there were just above 400, around 400, 450 towards the end of that period leading up to the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It was part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Therefore, a formation which is part of the JNA consisting of 400 men didn't have any wireless communication?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have it. I didn't see it. Therefore, I assume they didn't have it. It could be that somebody else had it and I didn't know about it. That's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Very well. We'll move away, then, from the 17th and let's go to the 18th of April, 1992. You have described two essential tasks that were undertaken by the 4th Detachment, firstly was the securing of border areas around the Bosna River and the collection of illegal weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you've given evidence of later collection of weapons by the 4th Detachment. In the course of that collection of weapons, were legally possessed weapons seized?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go with the soldiers who were assigned to collect weapons. I said that illegal weapons were confiscated, so during that first period of time, they probably did not confiscate legally possessed weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You gave detailed evidence of the consensual nature of the seizures. You gave detailed evidence of the manner in which soldiers from the 4th Detachment simply asked for weapons to be handed over and you gave evidence that houses were not entered or searched by soldiers of the 4th Detachment. How were they to obtain illegally possessed weapons if they weren't entering houses and searching?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said how they could have done it. The explicit orders of the commander were to collect illegally possessed weapons without forcing anyone to surrender weapons. So simply two or three soldiers would come two or three soldiers covering that area, and they would go door-to-door and say hello, good afternoon, do you have any illegal weapons? And then the other person would say no. And then they would go to the next door, and so on. That's the way that this went on. A large number of people did have weapons and took it out and turned it over to the members of the 4th Detachment. Sometimes they would say, well, it's owned by my father, it's owned by my brother, without saying that it was actually owned by them and this is how they found a way of surrendering weapons to the members of the 4th Detachment. I can give you an example. We've already heard a witness testify here and saying that members of the 4th Detachment came to his house. The witness is called Galic -- Galib Nurkic, and he's an uncle of Saban -- Hasan Subasic. According to the records, in our possession, we knew that Galib Nurkic was not a member of the HDZ and did not have weapons. When they came to see him and asked him whether he had weapons he replied no. And the people went on. The following day, he came to my house and complained to me, saying, "Brko, please help me, I lied yesterday. I in fact do have a rifle." I asked him, whose rifle it was and he said, "Don't ask me, you know whose it is." And then I said to him, "All right, Galib, my son will come with you, he will take the rifle and he will turn it over," and he doesn't say anything -- he doesn't have to say anything about the origin of the rifle and that's how it was. He took the rifle from him, he turned it over to the 4th Detachment, without saying whose it was, and as a result of that, Galib had no consequences. He was not detained for illegally possessing a rifle. This is how it was. And there were many similar cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How can you tell the Trial Chamber of these cases, how can you tell the Trial Chamber of the methodology used by the 4th Detachment when you said two or three questions ago that you didn't go with the soldiers who were assigned to search? How can you testify to all of this unless you were there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am testifying about the fact which is well known. It has nothing to do with any rules of the 4th Detachment, I'm just saying that the man came to me, he said he had a rifle, and that the -- this rifle was taken and surrendered but this other thing that I was saying about the 4th Detachment, these are facts that I heard at the meeting, the meeting of the command of the 4th Detachment, when the commander was issuing individual orders. He wasn't issuing orders to soldiers. He was issuing orders to company commanders, and I was present there because I also was expecting to get an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. So your testimony that the 4th Detachment didn't enter houses, simply asked people to hand over illegal weapons, that's all based on orders that you heard being given on the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So therefore you can't tell us if any of the testimony of the Prosecution witnesses who described forcible searches of their premises is correct or incorrect, you weren't there.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present when the statements were made that I talked about, but so far I haven't said anything about anybody who did not hand over weapons or that there was any forcible seizure of weapons. I haven't come to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you of something else you said in evidence in chief. Mr. Lukic will find this at page 77. Again, your counsel, Mr. Lukic was asking you about the events of the 18th of April, in the course of your answer, you said this: So the commander told me, since the activities of the soldiers had already started, not only in the 4th Detachment but of others, that it would be necessary to see if it was possible to form a kitchen in the -- the text is unclear to me, but I believe you said Tekstilac. What I'm interested in is this: Who were the others who had started activities along with the 4th Detachment that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The others were the other soldiers, if there were any, but there were some from the other battalions, from the 18th, who arrived to secure this line, the line on the River Sava and the River Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What about paramilitaries from Serbia? Were they included in the others that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were also hungry and they had to eat somewhere too, but I think that they didn't eat at Tekstilac, I think that they ate at Uniglas, I'm not sure but this is implied. I said that this was a place where soldiers ate also police officers, including also clearly a large number of citizens who were able to find food there. Why would there be any exceptions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's plain from your testimony that at the very least on the 18th, the 4th Detachment was swinging into action and along with it, were other armed units of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say it like that, even though I don't have any detailed information about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And positions were being secured and adopted by the -- by these armed formations?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are pulling me into these powers of the commander. My task was of a different nature. The commander knows what he did and how he deployed the soldiers. I didn't have any insight into that. I can say that the positions were secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: These armed formations, the 4th Detachment and other armed formations of the JNA were, and I quote from your words, they had arrived to secure this line, the line on the River Sava, to secure it, correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can testify that it is so. What else would they be doing other than that? But these were not my duties, and I am just a man who knows that something was going on, and this is what I'm testifying about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your position that you knew almost nothing about what was going on. I understand that. But I still want to continue with this line of questioning, if I may. In order to secure positions and take positions, it would have required all sorts of endeavours by these armed formations, wouldn't it? For example, perhaps digging of trenches, parking of vehicles, setting up of posts, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as you are listing it, I could also say it, because neither of us are really experts on military issues. It is certain that positions had to be secured and this was done by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am following this line now but I object about questions which demand speculation. We all agreed yesterday also that Mr. Tadic is not a military expert, so if a question is asked about what could have been the tasks of the 4th Detachment in the Defence of town, then he should be asked whether he had heard if this happened or that happened, and not whether -- what the command should have had as its own task. He should be asked did he hear, had he heard, that the command was given such and such a task? Those would be the questions then that need to be put.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well, let me approach it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll approach it this way: On the 18th, 19th, 20th, 21st, and 22nd, 23rd, 24th, and 25th of April, did you see how the 4th Detachment and the other armed formations secured the line? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see that, but I knew that they were securing the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How many men were involved in this exercise of securing the line?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: While this operation of securing the line was conducted by these armed formations, were you, as logistics officer, assistant commander for logistics in the 4th Detachment, informed of any requirements relating to equipment such as raincoats, communication equipment, sandbagging requirements, armaments, weapons, repair to weapons, repair to clothing, shovels for digging holes, trenches, earth moving equipment to secure positions, equipment to remove obstacles and trees, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of that. I've already said here that when I came on the 18th to Tekstilac, that Mr. Mihajlo Tovirac was already there, who was working on these security matters as an expert [as interpreted]. He was a captain and a logistics person in the TO before the war. So he knew all of those military lines and he was carrying out those tasks at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: One correction in the transcript, because here on page 33, line 23 he was working security matters. This is not an accurate translation of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat what he said so that we have a correct translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that on the 18th, I said that yesterday or the day before, when I was talking about that, that when I arrived at Tekstilac to form the kitchen, this person, Mr. Mihajlo Tovirac was already there and another neighbour of mine who was also a reserve officer, and they were working on this securing. So they were experts for this job, because this Tovirac was a captain, I don't know whether Captain First Class, and before the war, he worked in the TO on those assignments, so he was dealing with this logistics securing and he knew very well what should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did the command in Pelagicevo that was responsible for logistics, inform you, the assistant commander of logistics in the 4th Detachment, of any developments or concerns relating to logistics?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't inform me about any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So therefore, tell me if I'm correct, Mr. Tadic, your role as assistant commander for logistics in the 4th Detachment was basically to organise food? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I never talked about that with the commander, but they probably assessed that I didn't have enough expertise to do that kind of work so they engaged that other man, not asking me about it at all, and they gave me tasks that I could perform successfully and which I knew how to do, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, can you tell the Chamber, can you explain to the Chamber, how it is that a man who doesn't have enough expertise to carry out the position of commander of logistics, assistant commander of logistics, gets that job? Do you know why? How that came about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how that came about, but I said that Mr. Bogdanovic felt that it would be the easiest for me to carry out that aspect of the reserve work, and that's what they gave it to me. They didn't give me other tasks because they knew that I wasn't expert enough to do that, and practically throughout that whole period before the 17th, I wasn't doing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn now again to the other aspect of the 4th Detachment's activities on the 18th and that's the collection of weapons. Did the 4th Detachment members who went about collecting weapons, as far as you know, of course, carry arms? Were they armed when they did that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see, I saw that the majority of the members of the 4th Detachment had weapons. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did they use vehicles, loudspeakers, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the 4th Detachment didn't have any vehicles. They didn't have loudspeakers, and the vehicle, that is being mentioned here, which was used with the loud speaker probably came from some detachment that did have such a vehicle. It must have been a motorised unit or something. As I said I'm not an expert, but there are infantry and motorised units. The infantry ones have only infantry and the motorised have the vehicles. So that probably came from some unit, a motorised unit of that composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did any other military formations participate together with the 4th Detachment in this collection of weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the man who was doing the driving, and I don't know if anybody was with him together in the vehicle, but he wasn't from the 4th Detachment, because the 4th Detachment didn't have such a vehicle. I don't know. I didn't see that man so I don't know which unit he was from. Perhaps someone else can tell you that, somebody who is better informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Do I take it from that last answer that you gave that the 4th Detachment performed this collection of weapons by itself, apart from the appearance of this one stranger driving around in a car? Is that correct? Or vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In your first question, you didn't mention the 4th Detachment, but just the vehicle, and I said that the 4th Detachment mainly collected the weapons from the 4th neighbourhood, the sector, so I knew about it, I found out about it and I -- it might have appeared somewhere there but this vehicle never came to the 4th district. I don't know what the collection of weapons was like in the other districts other than what I have already told the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, I don't seem to be getting the answer that I want. I'll repeat the question that I asked three questions ago so that you understand it. Did any other military formations, plural, military formations, participate together with the 4th Detachment in this collection of weapons? If you know of any other military formations please tell the Chamber which formations they were.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 4th district, no. As far as any other organisation is concerned, I don't know, except if you want me to tell you what I heard here in this Chamber. I know that there was a vehicle which was involved in the collection of weapons, but I never dealt with that much, and I know that it did not belong to the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did the Serbian volunteers participate in searches, going from house to house, seizing weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time from which zone they were -- in which zone they were collecting the weapons. I found out about that here, that they were collecting them, and that they were entering houses. I don't have any knowledge that they were doing it in the 4th district. Perhaps much later. But at the time I don't have any knowledge that they were entering the 4th district.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. So your position to the Trial Chamber is this, Mr. Tadic: You had to come here to The Hague to find out -- listen to this trial, hear the evidence, to find out that the paramilitaries went around searching people's houses and seizing weapons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not claiming anything that I don't know. I'm saying that at that moment, I didn't know where those members of the Special Forces, let me call them that way, were collecting weapons because I was focused on the 4th district. I perhaps knew about it one month later, but that doesn't mean anything if I found out that, for example, they were collecting weapons in some other district. The details about them entering houses is something that I heard about in this courtroom. I didn't know about that before. So I'm not claiming anything specifically. What I know is what I claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll put the question in the simplest of terms. When did you ascertain, find out, that the paramilitaries had participated in searching houses and seizing weapons? When did you first become aware of that in time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I never ascertained which houses they entered, and what weapons they seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not asking which houses. I'm not asking which houses, Mr. Tadic. It's very simple. When did you find out that the paramilitaries had participated in searches and seized weapons? That's all. Did you find out about it on the 18th, on the 16th, on the 17th? Did you find about it a decade later here at the trial? When did you find out about it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a specific date, but you must know that information that I have received over the past nine years are all intermingled. How can I know when I remembered or when I found out from somebody what happened? It's impossible to determine the date. Perhaps I heard that in May or perhaps in July, but I don't have any personal knowledge about the things that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Zaric was in the town on the 17th and 18th of April, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, on the 17th, also based on my information, he went to Pelagicevo and the other days he spent in Samac. I don't know where he was specifically but I assume that he was in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: He was asked questions on this topic by investigators from the OTP. I'm referring -- I'll quote to you now from Exhibit P141, that's P141, not P141 ter. It's the English-only version and I'll read out to you what Mr. Zaric had to say on this issue. Page 13. "There is something that is also very important for Mrs. Nancy to know. It wasn't just the 4th Detachment that was going and disarming people in order to prevent a further conflict but also members of Serbian police, those in camouflage uniforms also went to disarm people, and they were doing it in a very different way. They were entering and searching houses and they were detaining people, not only were they doing it but they were also doing it to some members of the 4th Detachment as well. What happened is very important to see. The separation of these two different forces in town and that sometimes members of the 4th Detachment who had their weapons issued legitimately were still being disarmed by the Serbian police and the people in camouflage uniforms" and he goes on to describe the process. So he was aware of this -- of the fact that the men in camouflage uniform, the Sareni, were participating in searches and going into houses, arresting people. Is there any explanation for why he would have that information and you wouldn't, that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The explanation is very simple. Mr. Zaric was an officer for intelligence and security affairs, so he has no idea how I formed the kitchen. It's a completely different area from what he does. So as an officer for security, and as an experienced policeman, he learned of all of those details, which are a part of his work. The part of my work that I was carrying out is something completely different. I wasn't trained and I didn't know how to carry out the jobs that he was doing, so I don't know what he -- the job that he was carrying out and he doesn't know the job that I was carrying out. They are two separate jobs, two separate men, and men -- two separate men with completely different interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You would agree of course that the appearance of camouflage men from Serbia in the town conducting searches is a matter that would excite the interest of military commanders? Particularly in the 4th Detachment? No matter what their task?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment. Again, this is speculation, the way this question is phrased. The witness should be asked if he had heard that the commanders of the 4th Detachment were concerned about this. The way the question is put now calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well, I'll withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, you've given very clear evidence that the 4th Detachment, as far as you could tell, did apparently nothing on the 17th but sprang into action on the 18th. I want to put to you something that Mr. Zaric had to say concerning the dates. And I refer to Exhibit P140 ter. He was again being asked about events on the night of the 16th and 17th of April, and he said -- in fact to save time perhaps I could ask the registry to produce P140 ter it will save time and the reference, Mr. Tadic, you will find at page 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the question just put by the Prosecutor, that he said that Tadic had stated that 4th Detachment had no tasks on the 17th. Could the Prosecutor tell us where did Tadic stated that. He said something about the weapons on the 17th but I don't think that was the answer Mr. Tadic gave to my question but let Mr. Prosecutor tell us that so that we can locate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, that's the effect of his evidence. He's described already what happened on the 17th, the telephone call in the morning, told to do nothing, and he agreed with me, I used the expression springing into action, I recall distinctly a few moments ago, that they sprang into action on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell best about what I stated. I said that I didn't, but I also said that the commander, upon coming from Pelagicevo, deployed the 4th Detachment in accordance with the order so it's not that I said that the 4th Detachment was not ordered to do anything. I said that the commander, upon coming there, was given orders to deploy the 4th Detachment. I said that I didn't have to go anywhere to see whether there was going to be an attack or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: There is no challenge to that. There is no challenge to that. We are all clear. On the 18th, searches started, on the 18th, the kitchen started. On the 18th, positions were secured. On the 17th, Mr. Tadic was given no orders to do anything. There is no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Di Fazio put the question as follows: That Tadic had to conclude that the 4th Detachment did nothing on the 17th and on the 18th. That was the question put by Mr. Di Fazio, and Mr. Tadic gave the answer he gave me in examination-in-chief. That's why I wanted Mr. Di Fazio to tell me where exactly was this recorded by Mr. Tadic, because Mr. Tadic replied clearly to this, and I object to the way the question was put. Mr. Tadic gave an appropriate answer. The same answer he gave to me during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let me put it this way, Mr. Tadic. As far as you could observe, there were no significant military activities on the part of the 4th Detachment on the 17th. On the 18th, as far as you could determine, they did spring into action, starting with the searches, starting with the securing of the Bosna, all right? That's a fair assessment, wouldn't you say?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If your assessment is that it was in that way, then that is only strictly speaking your assessment but not a correct one. What I said is the correct assessment and you can find that in the transcript in several places.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Tadic. You tell the Chamber now, please, of all the significant military actions undertaken by the 4th Detachment on the 17th so that we are absolutely clear. Tell them what they did. Tell them what you saw and observed. Tell them if you saw men marching down the street, vehicles moving about, securing of positions, searching of weapons, et cetera, on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any of that and I didn't say that I had seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Now, P140, the interview of Simo Zaric on the 1st of April, 1998. In answering questions of the investigators, and you can read it for yourself because it's at page 449, he said that the role of the 4th Detachment was not to allow the transfer of war from Croatia -- I'm sorry, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll continue. He said that the role of the 4th Detachment was not to allow the transfer of war from Croatia, prevent interethnic clashes, had no function until the 16th and 17th, and then they started acting on the orders of the commander on the 17th of April at 8.00 in the morning after the Special Forces of the Serbian authorities and the volunteers from Serbia had already taken power in Samac. Now, plainly, his assessment is that an order for action came at 8.00, 17th of April. Are you aware of any such order for action at 8.00 on the morning of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information in this form, as presented by Mr. Zaric, is not something that I have. I wasn't responsible. I wasn't in charge, in order to justify, for me to know them. Let me repeat once again that my interests and that of Mr. Zaric are quite different. It would be the same as if you asked Mr. Zaric how to make an espresso coffee. He knows nothing of it, just as I know nothing of security issues, handled by an officer who was in charge of that in the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, did you ever experience any feeling of being kept in the dark about matters concerning the 4th Detachment in those days, following the 16th and 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no need to know about this, and I wasn't the person that was supposed to be informed in detail about this. I knew of things in a global form. I knew details of my own tasks but I didn't know any details concerning the tasks of those who were subordinated to the commander. That is something that only the person assigning tasks could have known, just as the person in charge of security matters, but how could I know of orders that were issued to the 1st Detachment or any -- or 1st company or any other unit? How could I know about that? Nobody had the duty to inform me of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I wasn't so much concerned about the 1st Detachment or the first company or any other unit, I was more concerned about the 4th Detachment. Did you have any view that you were being kept in the dark regarding activities of the 4th Detachment in the days following the 16th and 17th of April? That you were not being told things as assistant commander of logistics?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I'm saying things here, everything that I'm saying here pertains to the 4th Detachment. And I don't have the impression that you seem to have. I was sufficiently informed in the realm of things that I was supposed to be informed of, but nobody informed me, nor did they have the duty to inform me, about what the 1st company was doing or any other unit. Nobody officially informed me about that. I could see that people were behind the embankment, taking positions there, hiding and waiting to be issued orders, but that was not the official information. That was not -- that something informed me of officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well. Let me move to another topic. The -- do you agree that shots that were fired at your house when you were standing out on the balcony was for you a frightening and dangerous thing? For you personally.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there is shooting going on, that is definitely dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And it's something that you could -- sorry, do you want to take a glass of water or something?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. And it's something that you have not forgotten since it occurred, this shooting episode, and something that is indelibly etched into your memory?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be given Exhibit P138 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention, please, to page 34 and 35? But page 34 in the main, at the top. You can follow the exchange between yourself and investigators by simply looking at the B/C/S. I'll give you a moment to do that. All right. Okay, Mr. Tadic, there is only a couple of answers that I want to ask you about. You were asked by Nancy Paterson, who was then questioning you, who managed to take over the town of Bosanski Samac if the 4th Detachment was not involved? You replied it wasn't a problem to take over Bosanski Samac. Serbian police, some trained people in half an hour, they took over Bosanski Samac without any shots being fired, without shelling, without the war. And then you go on to comment on --
