utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what it says here, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It just says here, without any shooting. It didn't say without a single bullet being fired. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Read it out in whole, please, start at the beginning of the paragraph and read it out to the end, please. Slowly.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Well, it was no problem to take over power in Bosanski Samac, Serbian police with the assistance of some trained people took Samac in half an hour, without any shooting or war or shelling and so on."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That suits me, Mr. Tadic. So in 1998, 1998, when you were answering questions from the investigators, your position was there weren't shots fired, it all happened in half an hour. Why is it that you have told this Chamber that you heard shooting during the night, not only did you hear shooting during the night but that you personally, your house, was fired upon, your life placed in danger, because the two accounts cannot be reconciled.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They must be reconciled, because they did not take place simultaneously. Taking over of town took place in the morning, if I can say so, in the morning, between 2.00 and 3.00 a.m. whereas my house was shot at in the morning at 9.00 so -- and that event was totally unrelated to the taking over of power in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The thrust of your evidence has been clear. You didn't know what was going on at that particular time. You heard shots being fired from the direction of the river at night, and your house was fired upon later, perhaps in the morning -- in the morning. How and why do you make a distinction between those two events?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to make a distinction. I've just told you that the firing at my house had nothing to do with taking of the town, because the town had already been taken over at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You included that event when you were testifying to these Judges about the -- about the night of the 16th and 17th of April. You testified about having heard shots, being fired from the direction of the river, and then followed that with this description of shots being fired at your house. Plainly you were telling the Judges that was part of the events of the night and morning of the 16th and 17th of April. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I meant, if that was the conclusion drawn, then I have to tell you once again now that these two events have nothing in common. Taking over of town took place between 2.00 and 3.00 in the morning, whereas my house was shot at at around 9.00 in the morning, which means much later. The shooting at my house has nothing to do with the taking over of town. The people who shot at my house had already been in town, walking about town, they were in front of the health centre, and they probably felt some danger when they saw us appearing on the terrace. They perhaps expected us to shoot at them. In the town, that was already liberated, if I can call it that way. And this is why they shot several bursts that I've just described. So if the impression was created that these two events are somehow related, let me repeat once again, these two events have nothing in common.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Why do you call the activities of the night of the 16th and 17th a liberation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said conditionally speaking, liberated town, if I could call it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Well, was that your view back on the 16th and 17th of April, that Bosanski Samac had been liberated?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th and 17th of April, I believed that Samac had been taken and this is how I talked about it, that it had been taken by the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army and Territorial Defence. This is approximately how I described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get back to the central issue which I'm concerned about, namely what you said in the interview. Let's forget the shots that were fired at your house. Let's forget that. That's a separate episode, you say, unrelated. But your evidence here remains nonetheless that during the night, you heard shooting from the bridge, the direction of the bridge, or the river. Why did you tell the officers of the Office of the Prosecutor that the town was taken in half an hour without shots being fired, without any shelling, if in fact you had heard gun fire during the night?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This response here pertains to the context of war. If we were to speak about a war in Bosanski Samac, then we could say that Samac had been taken over in such a way that there was nothing dramatic about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the quote and the insistence of the Prosecutor that the witness stated on page 34 that there was no shooting at all, the immediately following response of the witness explains that there had been some shooting in fact, and therefore I don't think that the Prosecutor should insist at every particular word and should not take things out of context. I think that a general explanation needs to be given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's just what I said. If you are looking at it in a context of war, then you can say that it wasn't very intense, that gun fire was sporadic. I didn't claim ever that I heard a very intense gun fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, just so that the Judges can satisfy themselves as to whether or not I'm taking these remarks out of context, please read into the transcript the following question by Nancy Paterson and your answers, the following two. Sorry, I'll read the English and your answers into the transcript and you tell us if that's correct. Nancy Paterson question: There was no resistance offered by the non-Serbs? Answer: Mostly no resistance. Perhaps partly some but not significant. There is nothing there that I can see about shooting, gun fire, from the direction of the river.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly none. That means that there could have been some, perhaps partial. So it's not that there was absolutely nothing but it wasn't some major war, at least by my own assessment, I wasn't present there at the site, I'm not a military expert, but from a distance of kilometre and a half, that was the impression I had when speaking about the bridge. I wasn't present in town in order to be able to see what was going on there. That was the assessment that I had as a citizen sitting in his own house waiting for the events to develop.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, am I correct that we take our break at 1230?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to try and wrap this up before 12.30, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just go to page 36 of P138 ter, if you would, Mr. Tadic, page 36. And again, acquaint yourself with the questions and answers. Now, Mr. Tadic, in your answer at page 36, you said, that you would have moved your family out if you had known that there was going to be a takeover. In the morning, you were still at home, so we didn't know, as if nothing happened, because there was no shooting, and it's only when the commander told me that, that I then knew. Around my house, there were no buildings that needed to be taken over. There was, for instance, some bridge but that was far away from my house. The police station was also on the other side and was only when I went to the commander that's when I found out what had happened. Now, again, the reference to no shooting, is that what you meant to say in the interview?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wanted to say, I did say, namely that there were no activities around my house, and I said that all of those facilities that had been mentioned are quite distanced from my house and that's how it was. We were at home. My wife, my son and I. Therefore, nobody was removed elsewhere at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness was shown the document. However, when the Prosecutor started reading, he didn't read out everything. It says here that on the 18th of April, that day started normally, the 18th. That's the part that the Prosecutor did not read out to the witness. And the other part pertains to a completely different site.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here on that day, the 18th, meaning April, there was no activity going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, no, no. Just go up, go up to the -- to your answer at the top -- two-thirds of the way up the page. I'll read it. Nancy Paterson: So basically you went to bed on the 17th of April with absolutely no clue that the town was going to be attacked and at 8.00 the morning much to your surprise you found out that the town had now been completely taken over and was in control of the Serb forces. All right? Do you see that? Now, that's --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And that's a statement by Nancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, you know, and there is no dispute by you, that the town was in fact attacked on the 16th and 17th, the night of the 16th and 17th of April, correct? You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You know that it's the case of the Prosecution that the town was attacked and taken over on the night of the 16th and 17th of April. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You know that everyone is in accord that the takeover occurred or call it what you will, on the night of the 16th and 17th of April, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you just this: You either don't want to read this or you can't read. Does this mean that on the 17th of April, you went to bed and that the following day, at 8.00 in the morning you learned from the commander and so on. This here pertains to the 17th of April, when the town had already been taken over and I went to sleep and then the following day, at 8.00 in the morning I reported to the commander so there is nothing contentious here. This does not pertain to the night between the 16th and 17th. No. This refers to the 17th in the evening. Did you go to bed that night? This is where Nancy puts a question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Assuming that you're entirely 100 per cent correct, okay? Let's assume that, you still said it was as if nothing had happened because there was no shooting. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I've already stated, that there was no major war that could cause concern at that particular time. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, this is an appropriate moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will take our break or 20 minutes and resume at 1250 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, in your interview, again the one that we have been discussing, that's Exhibit P138 ter, taken on the 26th of March, 1998, you described the takeover of the town as a more of a kind of a political question, to prevent an interethnic conflict because there were indications that an interethnic conflict was going to happen. What precisely did you mean when you said it was more of a political question?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were indications that there could be a takeover of Samac on the part of forces from the Republic of Croatia. There were indications which were becoming apparent and that I talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, you've spent I suggest a good part of this morning telling the Trial Chamber that you knew virtually nothing of the 4th Detachment's intentions or movements on the 17th and you only found out on the 18th what was to happen. How can you say that there were indications that there was going to be a takeover from the forces of the Republic of Croatia in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The indications, and I'm not talking about the 17th or the 16th of April, the indications existed for days and days before that, not on that specific day but these indications were something that was talked about even 15 days before that, that possibly something like this could come about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. And so this was known to you and to the command of the 4th Detachment, these indications?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about what I knew as a citizen, not as a member of the 4th Detachment. Members of the 4th Detachment who were informed from these tales, these stories, also knew that. Other citizens knew that, that there was a danger of something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you see the 4th Detachment making any plans to deal with such a danger?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 4th Detachment did not make any such plans, but the higher command probably had such plans and probably more information than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That must be pure speculation on your part given your state of ignorance on any contingency plans.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But your question is like that. You asked whether I knew. So I assume that that is what it was like. I wasn't in the command, nor did I make any plans. You asked me if I knew about any plans of the 4th Detachment, and I said that I knew that there were no plans in the 4th Detachment but that they probably existed in the higher command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. You were asked by Nancy Paterson, page 34 of P138 ter question: So who ordered this takeover, if it was not a JNA action? Who gave the order for the takeover to occur? And you answered: Well, possibly the JNA command or the military police or the civilian police. I was not directly involved so I wouldn't know. Possibly the command. What --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have nothing to add to that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's okay. I'm not asking you to. I want to ask you a question about it. What made you say that it was possibly the JNA command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the JNA was - how can I put it - the one to prevent interethnic conflicts, and interethnic conflicts were a political question and that is why I thought that the JNA was in charge of preventing the interethnic conflicts in the regions where the JNA was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you ever form the view, in the days following the 16th and 17th of April, that the Crisis Staff had decided to take over the town with the help of the police and the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get such an impression then, or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And now, is that your position? Have you learned anything since the events of 1992 to lead you to the conclusion that the Crisis Staff decided to take over the town with the help of the police and the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please stop? Because the -- there is blood from the accused's nose. He's bleeding from the nose so perhaps we can take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it's nothing dangerous. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's not a question of danger. It's a question of the witness's comfort.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's better for us to make a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will have a break and we'll wait to be informed. --- Break taken at 1.01 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has been informed by the registry assistant that the accused who has been giving evidence is not well enough to continue because the nurse has indicated that the blood pressure is very high so the trial is not able to continue. We shall adjourn now and continue our proceedings on Monday, depending on the status of health of the accused. Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to address the Chamber officially. What worries me are two things: One, the willingness of my client to finish the proceedings as soon as possible, and as you were able to see over the past few days he did want to continue to testify, even though he was bleeding. The second concern is my professional concern, like I mentioned the other day, about his state of health and whether he's able to maintain the same concentration throughout the proceedings. We were informed by the Registry that upon our insistence, and upon the proposal of the Chamber, he would be examined by Dr. Falke in the detention unit and we expected this examination would be conducted on Friday after the proceedings so that we would all be able to find out what his state of health was, and whether he was able to go through testifying for the whole day, but the examination has not been carried out to this very day, and we were informed by the Registrar that steps have already been taken for this examination to be conducted this afternoon. I remember the same thing happened about a year ago, when Mr. Tadic was taken ill. So unfortunately, until we took steps via the Chamber to make sure that he was examined, he was not examined by a doctor. So in circumstances like these, where he's testifying the whole day, he really does need to go through a medical examination, and if it's necessary, we are asking for the assistance of the Chamber to help us secure this medical examination, because it really is important for Mr. Tadic to finish his testimony. He just managed to tell me now while he was waiting to be examined that his blood pressure is even higher than it usually is, and he suffers from high blood pressure any way. Any way, I'm going to get in touch with the Registrar to see whether there would not be any more serious consequences relating to him completing his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. The Trial Chamber will take steps through the Registry to see to that he's medically examined and so that the Trial Chamber is informed as to whether or not he can continue at this stage with his testimony. The Court will adjourn and the proceedings will continue on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: 1.22 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 24th day of February, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
